name: Kaus Australis
description: A star 44 parsecs away spinning at 99.5% or more of its break-up rate: its equator is 1.46 times wider than its poles.

radius.source: Bailey et al. (2024), ApJ 972, 103, Table 5, the model the paper calls Best: equatorial radius 8.80 (2-sigma range 8.47 to 8.89) and polar radius 6.01 (5.90 to 6.08) solar radii, from a rotating Roche model fitted to the star's polarization, its spectral-energy distribution, its projected rotation speed and the Hipparcos parallax; the record holds the volume-equivalent sphere of the two, 7.75 solar radii, and the scene draws the flattening

temperature.source: Code, Davis, Bless & Hanbury Brown (1976), ApJ 203, 417, HD 169022: effective temperature 9460 +/- 220 K (Table 6), from the measured angular diameter and the star's flux from the ultraviolet to the infrared

radialVelocity.source: Anderson & Francis (2012), Astronomy Letters 38, 331, XHIP, HIP 90185: RV -15 +/- 3.7 km/s (quality B)

distance.source: Anderson & Francis (2012), Astronomy Letters 38, 331 (XHIP), Hipparcos astrometry, HIP 90185: the Hipparcos parallax (van Leeuwen 2007) the radius is computed with, 22.76 +/- 0.24 mas, inverted

position.credit: Anderson & Francis (2012), Astronomy Letters 38, 331 (XHIP), Hipparcos astrometry

record.source: Bailey et al. (2024), Epsilon Sagittarii: An Extreme Rapid Rotator with a Decretion Disk, ApJ 972, 103 (https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ad630b; https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.11352), Table 5 (Best-fitting Stellar Parameters), column Best, and Table 4 for the position angle, read from the authors' LaTeX source
record.caption: Best-fitting Stellar Parameters. The parameters listed are those of the grid model giving the lowest chi-squared among all models (Best), and the best model at inclination of 90 degrees. Range is the full range of stellar parameters corresponding to the 2-sigma region of the fit. Each grid model fits the spectral-energy distribution and the projected rotation speed at the Hipparcos parallax of 22.76 mas; the polarization chooses among them.

omega.cell: 0.999 (Best); range (2 sigma) 0.995 -- 1.0. The value is the centre of the last bin of the grid, where no error can be determined (Table 4, notes)

law.cell: Section 3.1: the rotating star is a Roche model whose gravity darkening follows Espinosa Lara & Rieutord (2011)

polePositionAngleDegrees.cell: theta_rot (deg) 39.9 (Table 4, the variant with a disk and up to 100 ppm of interstellar polarization, which holds the Best model; no error printed; the other variants give 39.9, 39.9 and 40.1)

edgeOnModel.cell: Table 5, column i=90: omega 0.997, T_p 11791 K, T_e 7884 K, R_p 5.98, R_e 8.59 solar radii, P_rot 1.63 days
edgeOnModel.note: The paper lists this model beside Best and says the star's strong shell absorption 'might favour a higher-inclination model' like it (section 3.5). The record draws Best, the lowest chi-squared.

disk.cell: p_disk 367 ppm (Table 4): a wavelength-independent polarization from a low-density edge-on gas disk (abstract)
disk.note: The decretion disk is not drawn.

record.note: A fit to polarization, not to an interferometric image: the paper calls the star 'an excellent candidate for observation by interferometry' (abstract). Polarization gives the axis's position angle, not which end of it leans toward us, and the star is seen nearly equator-on. The uncertainties are the larger side of the paper's 2-sigma ranges. The temperatures follow the law of Espinosa Lara & Rieutord (2011), which has no exponent; from the printed rotation rate and pole it gives a 7434 K equator against the printed 7433 K, and 7884 K against the printed 7884 K for the edge-on model (packages/bake/src/objects/stellar/gravity-darkening.test.mts). The same table gives a mean effective temperature of 9950 K, a mass of 3.80 solar masses and a rotation period of 1.61 days (38.6 hours).

text.card: A star spinning at 99.5% or more of its break-up rate, the highest yet measured in our galaxy.
text.introduction: Its polarized light fits a star of equatorial radius 8.8 solar radii and polar radius 6.0, with poles near 11,700 K and an equator near 7,400 K.
text.locator: Abstract (rotation rate); Table 5, column Best: R_e, R_p, T_p, T_e

notes: The edge-on model Bailey et al. (2024) list beside their best one (0.997 of the break-up rate, inclination 90 degrees, a 7,884 K equator), which they say the star's shell absorption might favor
The thin gas disk around the equator that the paper infers from the polarization and the spectrum
Which end of the axis leans toward us: polarization gives the axis's position angle, 39.9 degrees, not its sense, and no interferometric image of the star exists
